conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hello, I'm Dr. Lee. I’ll be overseeing your care during this admission. Can you tell me what brought you in today?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Hi, Doctor. I’ve been having more frequent low blood sugar episodes—almost daily—and I keep getting confused. I even sent an email to my specialist that I don’t remember writing.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That sounds concerning. These episodes—do they come with dizziness, memory loss, or nausea?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, all of those. And I’ve been dry heaving a lot, though not actually vomiting. My stomach pain has come back too, like the ulcers I had before.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I see. You're on diazoxide now instead of octreotide, and your tube feeds were adjusted recently. But things aren’t improving?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Right. I was doing well until I came back from my trip. Then the lows started again, and the constipation returned even though I’m eating high-fiber foods.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Okay. We’ll check your G-tube site, run some labs, and consult neurology and endocrinology. Your symptoms could be tied to hypoglycemia, but we need to rule out other causes.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will I need any procedures?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Possibly an endoscopy to check for ulcers or other issues in your stomach. But first, we’ll monitor your glucose and adjust your feeds.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your labs came back normal—no infection, liver issues, or electrolyte imbalances. Glucose was 93, which is stable for now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s good, but I’m still worried about the lows happening without warning.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re going to switch your tube feeding schedule. Instead of continuous, we’ll cycle them—20 during the day, 40 at night—to see if that helps stabilize your sugar.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will that help with the nausea too?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Possibly. We’re also changing your anti-nausea med from Zofran to Compazine, which may work better for you.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Neurology reviewed your case. They don’t think you’re having seizures. Your confusion and memory lapses are likely due to the hypoglycemia.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That makes sense. But how do we stop the lows from happening?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll try a monitored fast tomorrow. We’ll stop daytime feeds around 1 PM and check your glucose. If it drops below 55, we’ll draw special labs to understand what’s going on.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What if it doesn’t drop?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Then we’ll know your body is maintaining sugar okay during fasting, and we can focus on adjusting meds and diet.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. How are you feeling? Any symptoms overnight?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No lows, actually. I did have some dry heaving, but not as bad as before.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Great. Your fingerstick this morning was 88. We’ll start the fasting study today at 1 PM.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re stopping your daytime tube feeds now. We’ll check your glucose every 30 minutes.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your glucose is holding at 78. That’s well above the threshold.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So no labs today?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Correct. But we noticed your glucose meter readings were inconsistent with actual fingersticks. We’ve replaced the meter and strips to ensure accuracy at home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Oh, I didn’t realize it could be off. That might explain some of the scary lows I thought I was having.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. We want you to have reliable tools. We’ll also schedule an endoscopy tomorrow to check your stomach and bypass anatomy.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You had the endoscopy this morning. The good news is no ulcers were found at the gastrojejunal anastomosis.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s a relief. What about the abnormal mucosa they mentioned?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: There are some changes in the esophagus and stomach lining, but nothing urgent. We’ll continue your pantoprazole twice daily to protect the lining.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And the metronidazole for bacterial overgrowth?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re stopping it for now. The GI team felt it wasn’t clearly helping, and we want to simplify your regimen.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The nutrition team met with you, right? They went over adding complex carbohydrates by mouth.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, they suggested oatmeal, whole grains—things that digest slowly. I think I can manage that.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good. That, combined with nighttime tube feeds only, should help prevent rapid glucose swings.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your glucose has stayed above 78 the entire time. No episodes of hypoglycemia in the hospital.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s really encouraging. Does this mean I can go home?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re planning for discharge tomorrow. We’ll finalize your new medication and feeding plan.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good news—you’re cleared to go home today. Your mental status is clear, and you’ve been stable.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What changes should I expect in my routine?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ll run tube feeds only at night—from 11 PM to 7 AM—at a rate of 40. During the day, you’ll eat complex carbs and avoid simple sugars.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my medications?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Diazoxide will now be taken three times a day—25 mg at breakfast, 25 mg at dinner, and 50 mg at bedtime. We’re also switching your sleep med to zolpidem.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What about the nausea?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ll have prochlorperazine—5 mg up to four times a day as needed. Take it at the first sign of nausea.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And follow-up?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ll see Dr. ___ in three weeks. Call sooner if you have severe lows, persistent nausea, or confusion.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you, Doctor. I feel much more confident about managing this now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. We’re here if you need us. Take care, and follow the plan closely.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Just a quick check before discharge—your G-tube site looks stable. The hypergranulation tissue is still there, but not infected.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Should I continue the mupirocin?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, apply it twice daily as before. If it gets worse, let your surgeon know.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your discharge paperwork is ready. The nurse will go over everything, including your new feeding schedule and meds.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ll make sure to review it all before I leave.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: One last thing—your mental clarity has improved significantly. That’s likely because your glucose is stabilizing.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I feel more like myself. I hope this continues at home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We do too. Stick to the plan, monitor your sugar with the new meter, and call if anything changes.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The transport team will take you home in about an hour. Do you have any final questions?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No, I think I’ve got it all. Thank you for your help.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. Take care, and we’ll see you at your follow-up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Just confirming—you understand when to take each dose of diazoxide?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes—25 mg with breakfast, 25 mg with dinner, and 50 mg at bedtime.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Perfect. And remember, the nighttime tube feeds start at 11 PM, rate 40, until 7 AM.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Got it. I’ve written it down to be sure.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your ride is here. We’re discharging you now. Please follow up as scheduled.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you, Doctor. I appreciate all your help.
